newsitem.title: USA: Facing new competition, Guitar Center rocks on.
newsitem.headline: Facing new competition, Guitar Center rocks on.

text.p: Guitar Centre Inc. is rocking on with plans to take its music superstores nationwide despite a new competitor that wants to grab the spotlight in the $5.6 billion music products market.

"We had $213 million in sales last year, which is a small part of the overall $5.6 billion music products market. There's ample opportunities for growth," Chief Financial Officer Bruce Ross said in an interview.
In its first quarterly financial report since the 31-store chain went public in March, Guitar Centre on Monday reported better-than-expected sales of $59.8 million.

The 33-year-old Agoura Hills, Calif.-based company earned $1.7 million, or 8 cents a share, up from $1.2 million, or 6 cents a share, on a restated basis a year earlier to reflect its public offering and other items. Comparable-store sales rose 13.6 percent.

Ross said comparable-store sales in the current quarter were running at around the same rate. He also said he was comfortable with analyst estimates for second-quarter earnings of 10 cents a share on a pro forma basis and full-year earnings of 50 cents a share.

A week before Guitar Center's initial public offering -- which made it the lone public company in the fragmented retail rock 'n' roll products market -- former Office Depot Inc. President Mark Begelman launched another giant music chain: privately held Mars Inc.
Several analysts have initiated coverage on Guitar Centre with buy recommendations, citing a strong outlook for the company, but also raising concerns about Begelman's entry.

"Good luck to him," said Ross, referring to Begelman. He said Begelman's concept differs from Guitar Center's in that it has 35,000-square-foot stores, twice the size of Guitar Centre stores, and carries sheet music and other products not carried by Guitar Centre.
Ross said he was confident that Guitar Center's market dominance will persist.

"There are barriers to entry, such as whether he'll (Begelman) get supplies from all vendors. We don't think so," said Ross. "We've been in business for a long time and we have long-established relationships."
Another competitor is Sam Ash, but that chain is mainly in New York and Guitar Centre has no immediate plans to enter that market, Ross said.
In addition to solid vendor relationships and its reputation for deep discounts, Guitar Centre is known as "the store" for music industry stars.
In any given week at its flagship store in Hollywood, hit musicians like Alanis Morissette and members of the band Aerosmith come in to shop.
Ross said about 35 percent of revenues come from sales to professional musicians, while aspiring musicians account for about 45 percent and hobbyists 20 percent.

The sales force is predominantly musicians. "We want musicians to be comfortable with our stores. They (salespeople) speak the same lingo and dress the same way and that's why our concept works so successfully," he said.
He said 95 percent of Guitar Center's customers are male between the ages of 18 and 34.
Guitar Centre has said it plans to open eight new stores this year and next year.

"We intend to remain a high-growth retailer, so we will do whatever we need to achieve annual growth sales between 25 and 30 percent," said Ross. "Come 1999, we have to open 10 or 12 stores to maintain that growth rate. We will."
In the first quarter, Guitar Centre opened four stores. Since the quarter ended, it has announced the acquisition of Rhythm City, with two stores in Atlanta.
Guitar Centre stock fell 12.5 cents to $14 in midday trading on Nasdaq.
